Jalen Hurts played a full NFL game in London with a blood clot in his calf, and the doctors who cleared him made that call because running around on it was safer than sitting still.

The eight-hour flight home was the part they were worried about. By Wednesday night, the clot had moved.

It comes down to how blood gets out of your legs. Pushing blood down to your feet is easy for the heart. Getting it back up means fighting gravity, and your calf does most of that work. Every contraction squeezes the veins running through the muscle and pushes blood upward past a chain of one-way valves, which is why vascular doctors call the calf your second heart.

Clots tend to form where a damaged vein meets blood that's sitting still, and a Rams cleat supplied the damage on October 4th.

He practiced in full that Wednesday and Thursday, then asked for treatment on the calf, and the team flew to London. A Saturday ultrasound found a superficial clot. The Eagles' staff and doctors in London reviewed it and decided activity and mobility mattered most, so the medical plan for a blood clot in a quarterback's calf was to go play quarterback.

Then came roughly eight hours in an airplane seat over the Atlantic. Doctors had already asked for a follow-up ultrasound within 72 hours of the game and the flight back, which tells you exactly which part of the trip they feared.

The World Health Organization's travel study found that sitting still for four hours or more roughly doubles your risk of a clot in your veins, and the elevated risk hangs around for about four weeks, so back-to-back flights stack. For a healthy traveler the absolute odds are small, around 1 in 6,000. Hurts boarded two transatlantic flights inside of a week with an injured vein.

"Superficial" sounds reassuring, and mostly it is. Those veins sit right under the skin. The deep veins run through the muscle and drain toward the heart and lungs, and that's where clots turn dangerous. In a French study of 844 patients with superficial clots, about 1 in 4 already had a deep clot or a clot in the lung at diagnosis. A separate study tracking 263 patients found 11% saw the clot spread into the deep system.

So "movement" is the one word in that statement that took him off the field.

The treatment may end up setting his timeline more than the clot does. Blood thinners are the standard answer, and doctors generally keep contact athletes off the field while they're on them, because a routine hit can turn into internal bleeding.

Chris Bosh went through this back in 2015. His clot started as what looked like a calf strain, took about two months to diagnose, and reached his lung. He missed Miami's final 30 games that season. A second leg clot a year later put him back on blood thinners, and he never played another NBA game.

Hurts got an ultrasound six days after the hit and a second one three days after the game. He's sitting out Sunday because somebody in London insisted on checking twice.
